correctness.rationale: For a pure three-complex the double is a graph. Each tetrahedron creates three distinct double-edges. In a facet stellar subdivision, the four new original edges yield four new double-vertices, three old opposite-pair edges are deleted, and four new tetrahedra create twelve distinct double-edges. The local replacement is the connected six-edge subdivision of K4, with the six original pair-vertices as subdivision midpoints, so exactly k old components merge. Thus ΔV=4, ΔE=9, Δc=1−k and Δβ1=6−k over the integers; k lies between one and three because the removed edges are three disjoint opposite-pair edges. The boundary of a four-simplex doubles to connected KG(5,2) (10 vertices, 15 edges, β1=6). Every stacked four-polytope is obtained by n−5 such facet operations and stays connected, giving β1=5n−19 and a circle wedge. The standalone verifier independently reconstructs these moves for 6,646 distinct stacked facet sets through nine vertices and 1,002 other cases. All quantifiers and boundary n=5 are covered symbolically; finite checks are only corroboration.

value.rationale: The double is a newly studied functor on simplicial complexes whose connectivity can depend strongly on the specific triangulation. The theorem gives an exact local topological calculus under the fundamental one-to-four tetrahedral refinement, including how many components merge, rather than only a face-count computation. Its all-size stacked-four-polytope corollary establishes a nontrivial connected homotopy classification independent of stacking history and a sharp five-circle increase per operation. Juxtaposition with the known cyclic-four-polytope parity split shows a mathematically meaningful sensitivity among triangulated three-spheres, a natural question not resolved by the general weak Cohen--Macaulay connectivity theorem.
